newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korean defectors dispel spy agency rumours.
newsitem.headline: North Korean defectors dispel spy agency rumours.

text.p: Two North Korean families who defected to South Korea met journalists for the first time on Thursday to try to clear up suspicions that their flight was staged by a Seoul intelligence agency.
Suspicions were fuelled after two Korean newspapers splashed exerpts from the diary of a 13-year-old boy detailing the escape.
The exerpts were a gripping account of a daring crossing of a frozen river into China -- but the handwriting was different. One was an adult's script, the other childlike.

Some newspapers alleged the Agency for National Security Planning, the domestic spy agency, had deliberately created a stir by bringing in the defectors to divert attention from strikes battering the government this month.
"I took short notes when we were escaping to let people know about our journey," the boy, Kim Hae-kwang, replied as journalists pelted him with questions.
He said his mother, elder brother and himself made several copies to hand around.

Eyebrows were also raised when television pictures showed the two families looking fit and radiant and wearing colourful winter jackets as they stepped off a coast-guard helicopter following a harrowing sea voyage from China.
The group of eight -- a father and his three children plus a family of four -- were plucked by helicopter from a deserted island where they were supposedly dropped off by a Chinese boat.
Yu Song-il, the father of three, said the jackets were bought in China so the group would not attract attention with their shabby Korean clothes.
His mother died and his wife ran away after the South Korean embassy in Beijing said it could not assist his family because of Seoul's diplomatic ties with Beijing, Yu said.
He said the two families left North Korea separately and were helped through China by ethnic Koreans who gave them work and shelter. They met for the first time on the boat.
Thousands of North Korean escapees are rumoured to be living in China and Russia, awaiting their day to defect to South Korea.
The news conference was sponsored by the Agency for National Security Planning.
